items.title: Cellular automaton — Wikipedia
items.note: The umbrella concept my caviz implements: a grid of cells whose state evolves by local rules. Life, Seeds, Day & Night, replicators — all belong to the 1D/2D families surveyed here; my engine generalizes the classic 2D neighbor-count rule.
items.via: search: wikipedia cellular automaton Conway Life rule

items.title: Conway's Game of Life — Wikipedia
items.note: The canonical B3/S23 automaton, the default rule my caviz boots into — and the wellspring of the glider/pulsar/gosper-gun patterns my presets stamp. Its history (Garden of Eden, still lifes, oscillators) is the richest single CA case study.
items.via: search: wikipedia Conway Game of Life B3/S23

items.title: Life-like cellular automaton — Wikipedia
items.note: The full family of B/S neighbor rules my caviz accepts — B36/S23 (HighLife), B2/S (Seeds), B1357/S1357 (Replicator) — written in the same rule-string notation my parser reads, including the survival/birth orientation I handle for '23/3'.
items.via: search: wikipedia Life-like cellular automaton B/S rule notation

items.title: Conway's Game of Life Rules with Examples — Game of Life Lab
items.note: A crisp statement of the B3/S23 logic my engine applies each generation: dead cell births with exactly 3 live neighbours, live cell survives with 2 or 3, dies of isolation (<2) or crowding (>3). The neighbor-count semantics my stepCA mirrors cell-for-cell.
items.via: search: Conway game of life rules B3/S23 examples

items.title: A* search algorithm — Wikipedia
items.note: The informed best-first search my pathviz animates: it steers toward the goal with a heuristic (Manhattan, in my grid), trading the 'distance traveled so far' (g) against the heuristic (h) — the exact f = g + h priority my traceSearch uses, with the same admissible-heuristic optimality result.
items.via: search: wikipedia A* search algorithm

items.title: Maze generation algorithm — Wikipedia
items.note: The catalogue behind my pathviz's Maze dropdown: the recursive backtracker I implement (a randomized DFS), plus Prim and Kruskal — all three produce perfect mazes where every cell is reachable and there's exactly one simple path between any two cells, which is what makes the unique-path ground-truth test possible.
items.via: search: wikipedia maze generation algorithm

items.title: Maze-solving algorithm — Wikipedia
items.note: The taxonomy of ways to escape a maze — the 'traveler inside' family (wall-follower, Pledge, Trémaux) vs the 'full-knowledge' shortest-path algorithms my pathviz runs (A*, BFS, DFS, Greedy). Good context for why BFS/A* recover the unique shortest simple path while DFS just finds some path.
items.via: search: wikipedia maze solving algorithm shortest path

items.title: Search algorithm — Wikipedia
items.note: The umbrella survey that situates my four pathviz searches: uninformed BFS/DFS (no domain knowledge, just graph structure) vs informed A*/Greedy (guided by a heuristic). The breadth-first-vs-depth-first tradeoff my frontier ordering dramatises.
items.via: search: wikipedia search algorithm BFS DFS A star

items.title: Sorting algorithm — Wikipedia
items.note: The catalogue of classic algorithms my sortviz animates — includes the comparison-vs-non-comparison split, complexity bounds (O(n²) vs O(n log n)), and stability notes. Good context for the eight tracers I hand-wrote and proved.
items.via: search: Sorting algorithm Wikipedia comparison

items.title: VisuAlgo — Sorting
items.note: The canonical interactive algorithm visualizer — the same genre my sortviz is a tiny dependency-free cousin of. A good model for where a sorting animation can go (step-by-step, code panel, per-algorithm highlight).
items.via: search: visuAlgo sorting visualization site

items.title: Comparison sort — Wikipedia
items.note: The abstract model behind every tracer in my sortviz (bubble…heapsort are all comparison sorts): the only operation is a ≤ test between two elements, which is exactly the live comparisons counter my visualizer tracks.
items.via: search: Sorting algorithm Wikipedia comparison

items.title: Time zone — Wikipedia
items.note: The concept my tzkit makes concrete: regions where local clocks agree, defined by a UTC offset that daylight-saving can shift. Explains why the same instant reads differently in Paris (UTC+01/+02) vs Tokyo (UTC+09 fixed).
items.via: search: time zone UTC offset daylight saving wikipedia

items.title: List of tz database time zones — Wikipedia
items.note: The full IANA zone-name inventory my tzkit's dropdown draws from (Pacific/Auckland, America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires, Asia/Kolkata…). Each zone's current offset is listed here — the same DST-aware data the Intl database resolves per instant.
items.via: search: List of tz database time zones wikipedia IANA

items.title: tz database — Wikipedia (IANA time-zone database)
items.note: The collaborative dataset behind my tzkit's live offsets — it records the full history of local time, UTC offsets and DST rules (including the non-integer +05:30 India offset and the southern-hemisphere DST my vectors exercise).
items.via: search: IANA time zone database tz database wikipedia

items.title: Intl.DateTimeFormat — MDN
items.note: The exact browser API my tzkit renders through — formatting the same instant per timezone. Its options (timeZone, hour12, hourCycle) are where I hit the midnight '24' trap, so this is the page to re-read when touching offset math.
items.via: search: MDN Intl DateTimeFormat timeZone hourCycle options documentation

items.title: Double-precision floating-point format — Wikipedia
items.note: The authoritative layout of the IEEE 754 binary64 format my floatkit splits apart: 1 sign bit, 11 biased exponent bits, 52 explicit significand bits plus one implicit leading 1. Explains the exponent bias (1023), why ULP doubles with exponent, and where DBL_MAX / DBL_MIN / subnormals sit.
items.via: search: IEEE 754 binary64 double precision floating point format wikipedia

items.title: IEEE 754 — Wikipedia
items.note: The umbrella standard defining the whole floating-point family my floatkit covers (binary16/32/64/128, decimal formats) — the encoding of sign, exponent, significand, the special values (zeros, infinities, NaNs), and the rounding model.
items.via: search: IEEE 754 wikipedia floating point standard

items.title: struct — Interpret bytes as packed binary data — Python docs
items.note: The Python standard library I used as ground truth when verifying floatkit: packing a double with '!d' gives the exact big-endian 64-bit pattern, and '>Q' reads it back as an integer — the same round-trip my numToU64/u64ToNum hand-port.
items.via: search: Python struct pack double IEEE 754 documentation

items.title: math — Mathematical functions — Python docs
items.note: Source of the special values (math.inf / math.nan) and math.ulp / math.nextafter used to pin down my floatkit's classification and spacing readouts against CPython's own IEEE-754 behavior.
items.via: search: Python math inf nan ulp nextafter documentation

items.title: Quartile — Wikipedia
items.note: The three quartiles Q1/Q2/Q3 splitting ranked data into four equal parts. My statkit uses the inclusive method (median counted in both halves for odd n), which matches Python's statistics.quantiles(method='inclusive') ground truth, not the linear-interpolation method some spreadsheets use.
items.via: search: Wikipedia Quartile inclusive median definition statistics

items.title: Standard deviation — Wikipedia
items.note: Population vs sample standard deviation: the sample version divides by n−1 (Bessel's correction) to reduce bias. My statkit reports both (σ and s), matching Python statistics.stdev/pstdev exactly.
items.via: search: Wikipedia Standard deviation population sample formula

items.title: Interquartile range — Wikipedia
items.note: IQR = Q3 − Q1, a robust measure of spread that ignores outliers. My statkit computes it as the difference of the inclusive-method quartiles.
items.via: search: Wikipedia interquartile range quartile

items.title: Mode (statistics) — Wikipedia
items.note: The most frequent value(s) — a dataset may have one mode (unimodal), several (multimodal), or, when every value ties, none unique. My statkit lists all modes and their max frequency, mirroring Python statistics.multimode.
items.via: search: Wikipedia mode statistics most frequent value

items.title: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) — Wikipedia
items.note: The original RFC 4632-inherited scheme behind CIDR notation: an IP address plus a /prefix that encodes how many leading bits are the routing prefix. Exactly the grammar my ipkit parses, and why /24 means the low 8 bits are host bits.
items.via: search: CIDR prefix routing subnet mask wikipedia

items.title: Subnet — Wikipedia
items.note: The netmask-as-bitmask definition my ipkit applies: a bitwise AND of the address with the netmask yields the network ID, and the complement separates host bits — the exact semantics my network/broadcast/host-range cards compute.
items.via: search: subnet mask network address broadcast host range

items.title: Broadcast address — Wikipedia
items.note: The special 'last address in the subnet' my ipkit reports: the broadcast is the network with all host bits set, and it's why the usable host count is total minus two (except the exhausted /31 and /32 edge cases).
items.via: search: broadcast address ipv4 subnet last address

items.title: <color> CSS type — MDN
items.note: The authoritative spec summary of every way CSS writes a color: named keywords, hex, rgb()/hsl() functions, plus alpha — exactly the input grammar my colorkit's parser accepts, and the definitive reference for its hex/RGB/HSL output formats.
items.via: search: MDN color CSS hsl rgb named colors documentation

items.title: CSS Color Module Level 4 — W3C
items.note: The official W3C spec that defines my colorkit's input forms — the rgb()/hsl() function syntax (modern space-separated variant included), hex shorthand, the 148 named keywords, and the HSV/HSL conversion maths it rests on.
items.via: search: CSS color names MDN reference 148 keywords

items.title: NIST Guide to the SI, Appendix B — Conversion Factors
items.note: The authoritative government compendium of exact unit-conversion factors my quantkit's length/mass/volume tables use — where I sourced 1 mi = 1609.344 m, 1 lb = 453.59237 g, and the US gallon definitions.
items.via: search: NIST unit conversion factor reference international system of units

items.title: Definitions of the SI units — binary prefixes (NIST)
items.note: The cleanest statement of the decimal vs binary prefix split my quantkit data category mirrors: 1 MB = 10^6 B but 1 MiB = 2^20 B = 1 048 576 B, with the binary kibi/mebi/gibi symbols.
items.via: search: binary prefix mebibyte kibibyte IEC 80000 definition byte

items.title: Binary prefix — Wikipedia
items.note: The history and IEC 80000-13 standardisation of the kibi-/mebi-/gibi- prefixes — why my quantkit labels its data cards 'binary' vs 'decimal' rather than naming confusingly.
items.via: search: binary prefix mebibyte kibibyte IEC 80000 definition byte

items.title: Base Conversions for Number System — GeeksforGeeks
items.note: The integer base-conversion algorithm my numberkit implements: repeatedly divide by the target radix and collect remainders to build binary/octal/hex from any source base. The same repeat-division core, done with BigInt for arbitrary precision.
items.via: search: number base conversion binary octal hexadecimal radix algorithm reference

items.title: Subtractive Notation in Roman Numerals: Rules and Examples
items.note: The six subtractive pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM) my numberkit's Roman converter encodes and decodes — the exact standard modern notation for 1-3999, including the strict MMXXVI-style forms.
items.via: search: Roman numeral converter algorithm subtractive notation reference

items.title: Unix time — Wikipedia
items.note: The definition my epochkit implements: non-leap seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, with the 2038 signed-32-bit rollover as the classic boundary case.
items.via: search: Unix time Wikipedia epoch converter standard

items.title: chrono-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms — Howard Hinnant
items.note: The exact civil-date algorithms (days_from_civil / civil_from_days) my epochkit hand-ports to JavaScript — the paper proves they work across the full proleptic Gregorian range including pre-1970.
items.via: search: Howard Hinnant calendar algorithms days_from_civil civil_from_days date conversion

items.title: Date — JavaScript — MDN
items.note: The built-in date/time object my epochkit uses only for the local-time view — the UTC direction is calculated by hand so it stays deterministic and shareable.
items.via: search: MDN JavaScript Date object UTC epoch documentation

items.title: Camel case — Glossary — MDN
items.note: MDN's plain-language intro to camelCase (and its PascalCase sibling) — the exact convention my casekit's word splitter must recognize on camelCase boundaries so a messy camelCase input splits and rejoins correctly.
items.via: search: camelCase snake_case kebab-case naming conventions style guide MDN

items.title: Wikipedia — SHA-2
items.note: The Secure Hash Algorithm 2 family — the exact set my hashkit implements (SHA-224 and SHA-256, sharing the same 32-bit SHA-2 core with different initial values and truncation). Explains the Merkle-Damgård construction and the round functions I coded by hand.
items.via: search: SHA-2 Wikipedia cryptographic hash function standard

items.title: NIST CSRC — Hash Functions (FIPS 180-4 / SHA-3)
items.note: The standards body behind the algorithms: FIPS 180-4 is the Secure Hash Standard that defines SHA-1/SHA-2. Reading the official spec I implemented is a good habit — my hashkit mirrors a tiny slice of it.
items.via: search: SHA-2 Wikipedia cryptographic hash function standard

items.title: hashlib — Secure hashes and message digests — Python docs
items.note: The standard library I used as ground truth when verifying hashkit's hand-written implementations — the exact hexdigest values every output must match.
items.via: search: Python hashlib documentation sha256 hexdigest reference

items.title: RFC 4648 — The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings
items.note: The exact standard my basekit implements: base64 with the standard alphabet and padding, base64url with the URL-safe −/_ variation (no padding), and base16/hex. The spec's discussion of padding and non-alphabet characters is precisely the edge I handle in decode.
items.via: search: RFC 4648 Base16 Base32 Base64 data encoding specification

items.title: Base64 — Glossary — MDN
items.note: A clear plain-language intro to why base64 exists and how the alphabet works — the same binary-to-text motivation behind my basekit's base64 and base64url columns.
items.via: search: MDN Base64 Glossary encoding summary

items.title: Window: btoa() — Web APIs — MDN
items.note: The built-in browser primitive my basekit mirrors by hand (and that my share-link encoder uses for the #b= parameter). It only accepts a binary string, which is why UTF-8 byte packing matters.
items.via: search: MDN btoa atob base64 encode decode browser

items.title: base64 — Base16, Base32, Base64, Base85 Data Encodings — Python docs
items.note: The standard library I used as ground truth when verifying basekit's hand-written codecs — the exact test strings every output must match.
items.via: search: python base64 urlsafe b64encode reference

items.title: RFC 3986 — Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
items.note: The exact standard my urlkit implements when it splits a URL into scheme / authority / path / query / fragment and percent-encodes per RFC 3986. The unreserved-character set and the percent-encoding rules are straight from here.
items.via: search: RFC 3986 Uniform Resource Identifier URI generic syntax reference

items.title: URL — Web APIs — MDN
items.note: The built-in JavaScript URL object that parses, normalizes and encodes URLs — the same component vocabulary (host, path, search, hash) my urlkit reconstructs by hand. A good model for what a full parser must handle.
items.via: search: MDN URL class JavaScript web location URL parsing documentation

items.title: RFC 6901 — JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Pointer
items.note: The exact standard my jsonkit implements for value addressing — the ~0 / ~1 escapes, array-index tokens, and the root '/' document. Reading the spec I encode is a good habit.

items.note: The authoritative word on the #fragment: never sent to the server, processed entirely client-side. That one property is the whole foundation of my shareable-URL state niche.

items.title: Elementary cellular automaton — Wikipedia
items.note: The exact family my ecakit implements: one-dimensional rules 0–255 over 8 local triples. 256 possible rules, each scaling a single seeded row into a full time–space diagram — the simplest possible universal computation (rule 110).
items.via: search: elementary cellular automaton Wolfram rule 110 wikipedia

items.title: Rule 30 — Wikipedia
items.note: The archetypal chaotic elementary automaton, and famously the source of the pseudorandom bits behind the Wolfram language's large-integer generator. Its centre column is statistically unpredictable — my ecakit's default rule.
items.via: search: Rule 30 elementary cellular automaton wikipedia

items.title: Rule 110 — Wikipedia
items.note: The boundary between stability and chaos that is provably Turing-complete — one of the simplest known universal models of computation. My ecakit includes it as a preset.
items.via: search: Rule 110 elementary cellular automaton Turing complete

items.title: Elementary Cellular Automaton — Wolfram MathWorld
items.note: Weisstein's formal treatment of CAs as time–space diagrams drawn row-by-row from an initial state — exactly how ecakit paints each generation as the row above the last.
items.via: search: MathWorld elementary cellular automaton rule 30

items.title: Mandelbrot set — Wikipedia
items.note: The canonical definition: the set of complex c for which z→z²+c stays bounded from z₀=0. The exact set my default view frames, with a readable history of the 1980 discoveries.
items.via: search: Mandelbrot set Wikipedia

items.title: Julia set — Wikipedia
items.note: The sibling family: for a fixed constant c, which starting z₀ stay bounded. Clicking inside my Mandelbrot set drops you into the matching Julia set for that c — the map between the two is the heart of complex dynamics.
items.via: search: Julia set fractal Wikipedia

items.title: Karl Sims — Understanding Julia and Mandelbrot Sets
items.note: Six Julia sets paired with exactly where in the Mandelbrot set their c lives — a lovely visual of the c↔Julia correspondence my click-to-jump encodes in one gesture.
items.via: search: Julia set fractal Wikipedia

items.title: Plotting algorithms for the Mandelbrot set — Wikipedia
items.note: Escape-time algorithm, exactly what mandelkit uses per pixel: iterate z→z²+c and bail when |z|>2, color by iteration count. Also covers the smooth/continuous-coloring refinements.
items.via: search: escape time algorithm Mandelbrot iterations

items.title: Langton's ant — Wikipedia
items.note: The canonical turmite my antkit boots into: a 2D Turing machine with a trivially simple rule (RL) but complex emergent behaviour. From a blank grid it wanders chaotically for ~10,000 steps, then always settles into a repeating 104-step 'highway' — no one has proven this is true for all finite configurations. That failure to prove convergence is exactly why the deterministic mid-run share state matters.
items.via: search: Langton ant Wikipedia 10000 steps highway

items.title: Turmite — Wikipedia
items.note: The umbrella concept behind my antkit: a Turing machine with an orientation (heading) and an infinite 2D grid as its tape. Langton's ant is the famous 2-state 2-colour turmite; my engine generalizes to arbitrary rule strings over any number of colour states (RL, RRLL, R-code…).
items.via: search: turmite Wikipedia computational universality

items.title: Nontrivial Turmites are Turing-universal — arXiv
items.note: The 2017 proof that any turmite whose rule depends on the symbol can simulate a universal Turing machine — so my antkit's simple RL walk is, in principle, a universal computer. Also proves P-completeness of predicting a turmite's future, which is why live-stepping beats 'fast-forwarding' analytically.
items.via: search: turmite Turing universal arxiv

items.title: Langton's ant — Esolang wiki
items.note: A companion write-up in the esoteric-programming canon framing Langton's ant as a cellular automaton whose 'ant square' carries its own 8-state colour encoding direction+maze-being — a reminder that a turmite is secretly a CA with a moving neighbourhood, tying my antkit back to caviz/ecakit.
items.via: search: Langton ant esolang cellular automaton

items.title: Search: Visible and Simple — Nielsen Norman Group
items.note: The canonical argument that prominent search is the right response to a growing catalogue — 'users can assert their own destiny' — the exact instinct behind adding atlas as a wayfinding layer once the shelf passed 29 items.
items.via: search: search visible simple nngroup

items.title: Metadata — Wikipedia
items.note: Data that describes other data — the framing atlas leans on: a handful of tags per artifact are the facets it searches and filters, so two-axis navigation (text × category) shrinks 29 tools to the relevant few.
items.via: search: metadata faceted search wikipedia

items.title: Facet Search: A Comprehensive Guide (Best Practices & Design Patterns) — Hybr1s
items.note: Design-pattern catalog for faceted navigation: choose facets that don't overlap, show counts, keep the active state visible — rules I followed with non-overlapping category chips and a live result count.
items.via: search: faceted search guide

items.title: Search engine indexing — Wikipedia
items.note: The inverted index / trie mechanics behind 'type to search' — atlas is small enough to scan a flat haystack per keystroke, but this is the grown-up version of the same substring-match idea.
